prompt: In some countries, cash is being replaced almost entirely by digital payment. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?
essay:
Several countries are now close to abandoning cash altogether, and some shops and buses no longer accept it. On balance I consider this a positive development, with the important qualification that the people it disadvantages are almost invisible in the figures used to justify it.

The benefits are easy to see and are widely shared. Digital payment is faster, cheaper to handle than notes and coins, and far harder to steal in quantity; a lost card can be cancelled while lost cash cannot. Businesses save the time and expense of counting, banking and insuring their takings. Because transactions leave a record, undeclared income and cash-in-hand employment become harder to sustain, and that same record gives ordinary households something they never previously had, which is a reliable account of their own spending.

The costs fall on particular groups rather than on everybody a little. Older people who never adopted smartphones, those without bank accounts, and anyone whose income is too irregular for a bank to want them are excluded from ordinary transactions rather than merely inconvenienced. A cashless system is also a single point of failure: a network outage stops commerce completely in a way that a few card terminals failing never used to. And every purchase becomes data belonging to somebody else. That data is valuable, and nobody has explained why the person who generated it should not own it.

I still think the direction of travel is right, because the gains are large and the exclusions are fixable. But they are only fixable deliberately, through a legal duty to accept cash or through basic accounts that are genuinely universal, and the countries that have simply allowed cash to disappear have not fixed them.
title: Cash disappearing in favour of digital payment
